steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: A multimeter measures voltage (parallel), current (series) and resistance (power off); always select the correct range and mode.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: An oscilloscope displays voltage against time, allowing measurement of amplitude, frequency, period and wave shape.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Oscilloscope controls: Y-gain (V/div) sets vertical scale; timebase (ms/div or µs/div) sets horizontal scale.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: The trigger control stabilises the display by starting the sweep at a consistent point on the waveform.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Q: An oscilloscope shows 4 divisions peak-to-peak with Y-gain set to 2 V/div. What is V_pp and V_rms (sine)? | Q: How should a multimeter be connected to measure current through a resistor? | Q: A sine wave has a period of 5 divisions at 0.2 ms/div. What is its frequency?

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: V_pp = 4 × 2 = 8 V. V_peak = 4 V. V_rms = 4/√2 = 2.83 V. | The multimeter must be connected in series with the resistor, with the correct current range selected. | T = 5 × 0.2 = 1 ms = 0.001 s. f = 1/T = 1/0.001 = 1000 Hz = 1 kHz.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: For oscilloscope measurements: count divisions carefully and multiply by the V/div or time/div setting. Always convert period to frequency: f = 1/T; make sure T is in seconds before calculating. When asked about multimeter use, specify the connection: voltmeter in parallel, ammeter in series. Remember V_rms = V_peak/√2 for sine waves only; do not use this for square or triangle waves. Mention trigger level and slope when explaining how to get a stable oscilloscope display.
